Plural-address refutation (παράσχετε/σώσατε) noted as unattested in Scripture per Origen.
Jn 16:23 variant aitēsēte/aitēsētai recorded; sense unaffected.

choices.why: hupokeimenon is 'substrate/subject' here; 'hypostasis' would smuggle fourth-century precision into a pre-Nicene anti-modalist clause.
apemphainon carries disgrace/unseemliness, stronger than atopon; Origen's verdict on plural prayer-address.
Prosopopoeia of Christ answering prayer-to-Christ advocates; direct speech preserves the parallel with 'Why callest thou me good?'.

lemmas.lexica: LSJ: called to one's aid; NT: Paraclete

pass_a_gloss: Strict prayer (proseuchē) belongs to the Father alone — not to any generated being, not to Christ — yet never apart from the High Priest sworn by oath. Plural-address prayer ('grant, save' in the plural) is self-evidently unseemly and unattested in Scripture. Jn 16:23-24 proves asking the Father in the Son's name. Worship (proskunēsis) differs from prayer: angels worship Christ, kings 'worship' Jerusalem, without prayer being offered. Christ himself, voiced by Origen, redirects prayer to the Father through the sympathizing High Priest and Paraclete, that adopted brothers pray with and through him.
